item.title: Elemental Analysis of a Sodium Chloride and Potassium Chloride Mixture
item.stimulus:
A chemist receives a 2.000 g white crystalline sample labeled as sodium chloride, NaCl. The chemist suspects that the sample may also contain potassium chloride, KCl. Assume NaCl and KCl are the only possible components. Elemental analysis of the entire 2.000 g sample gives the result shown below.

Quantity | Value
Mass of sample | 2.000 g
Mass of chlorine (Cl) in sample | 1.108 g
Molar mass of Na | 22.99 g/mol
Molar mass of K | 39.10 g/mol
Molar mass of Cl | 35.45 g/mol
item.model_answer:
(a) Molar mass of NaCl = 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44 g/mol. Mass percent Cl = (35.45 g ÷ 58.44 g) × 100 = 60.66% Cl.

(b) The sample's mass percent Cl = (1.108 g ÷ 2.000 g) × 100 = 55.40%. Pure NaCl would be 60.66% Cl (2.000 g of pure NaCl would contain 1.213 g Cl). Because 55.40% is lower than 60.66%, the sample cannot be pure NaCl, so the claim is incorrect. The value lies between that of pure KCl (35.45 ÷ 74.55 = 47.55%) and pure NaCl, consistent with a mixture of NaCl and KCl.

(c) Let x = mass of NaCl; mass of KCl = 2.000 − x. Molar mass KCl = 39.10 + 35.45 = 74.55 g/mol.
x(35.45/58.44) + (2.000 − x)(35.45/74.55) = 1.108
0.6066x + 0.9510 − 0.4755x = 1.108
0.1311x = 0.157
x = 1.20 g NaCl

(d) A sample of pure NaCl contains only one type of particle, NaCl formula units, each with one Na⁺ and one Cl⁻. Because every formula unit has the same composition, the ratio of Cl mass to total mass is the same in any sample, 60.66%. A NaCl–KCl mixture contains two types of formula units, and their relative numbers can vary from sample to sample. KCl formula units have a lower Cl mass fraction than NaCl formula units, so a sample with a larger proportion of KCl has a lower overall mass percent of Cl.
item.verification_python:
M_Na=22.99
M_K=39.10
M_Cl=35.45
M_NaCl=M_Na+M_Cl
M_KCl=M_K+M_Cl
assert abs(M_NaCl-58.44)<1e-9
assert abs(M_KCl-74.55)<1e-9
fNa=M_Cl/M_NaCl
fK=M_Cl/M_KCl
assert abs(fNa*100-60.66)<0.005
assert abs(fK*100-47.55)<0.005
assert abs(fNa-0.6066)<0.00005
assert abs(fK-0.4755)<0.00005
sample=2.000
Cl=1.108
assert abs(Cl/sample*100-55.40)<1e-9
assert abs(sample*fNa-1.213)<0.0005
assert abs(sample*fK-0.9510)<0.0001
assert abs((Cl-sample*fK)-0.157)<0.0005
assert abs((fNa-fK)-0.1311)<0.00005
x=(Cl-sample*fK)/(fNa-fK)
assert abs(x-1.197)<0.001
assert abs(round(x,2)-1.20)<1e-9
back=x*fNa+(sample-x)*fK
assert abs(back-Cl)<1e-9
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

parts.prompt: Calculate the mass percent of chlorine in pure NaCl. Show your work.

criteria.text: Mass percent of Cl in pure NaCl is 60.66%, from 35.45 g ÷ 58.44 g × 100.
criteria.evidence: Response computes the molar mass of NaCl as 58.44 g/mol and divides the mass of Cl per mole by it to get about 60.66% (60.7% accepted).
criteria.fix: Add the molar masses of Na and Cl for the formula mass, then divide Cl's molar mass by that total and multiply by 100.

parts.prompt: A student claims the sample is pure NaCl. Use the elemental analysis data and your answer to part (a) to evaluate this claim.

criteria.text: Rejects the claim: measured Cl mass percent is 55.40%, which is lower than 60.66% for pure NaCl, so the sample is not pure NaCl.
criteria.evidence: Response calculates the sample's Cl mass percent (1.108 g ÷ 2.000 g = 55.40%, or compares 1.108 g to the 1.213 g expected for 2.000 g of pure NaCl) and states that the mismatch means the sample is not pure NaCl. A comparison consistent with an incorrect part (a) value earns the point.
criteria.fix: Compute the sample's measured mass percent of the element and compare it numerically to the value for the pure compound before making a claim.

parts.prompt: Assuming the sample contains only NaCl and KCl, determine the mass of NaCl in the 2.000 g sample. Show your setup and report your answer with the correct number of significant figures.

criteria.text: Sets up a correct mass balance for chlorine, such as x(35.45/58.44) + (2.000 − x)(35.45/74.55) = 1.108, where x is the mass of NaCl.
criteria.evidence: Response writes an equation (or equivalent system of two equations) that expresses total Cl mass as the sum of Cl from NaCl and Cl from KCl, with the component masses summing to 2.000 g and correct Cl mass fractions (0.6066 and 0.4755).
criteria.fix: Let x be the NaCl mass, write 2.000 − x for KCl, and add each component's mass times its chlorine mass fraction to equal the total chlorine.

criteria.evidence: Response solves the mass balance to obtain 1.20 g of NaCl (values from 1.19 g to 1.20 g accepted), reported with units.
criteria.fix: Solve the linear equation carefully: subtract 0.9510 from 1.108, then divide by the difference in Cl mass fractions, 0.1311.

parts.prompt: At the particle level, explain why every sample of pure NaCl has the same mass percent of chlorine, whereas the mass percent of chlorine in NaCl–KCl samples can differ from one sample to another.

criteria.text: Pure NaCl contains only NaCl formula units with a fixed 1:1 Na to Cl ratio, so its Cl mass fraction is fixed; a mixture contains both NaCl and KCl formula units whose relative proportions can vary, so its Cl mass percent varies.
criteria.evidence: Response states both ideas: a pure substance has a single type of formula unit with a fixed composition, and a mixture has two types of formula units in variable proportions, which changes the overall Cl mass percent (for example, more KCl lowers it).
criteria.fix: Describe what particles each sample contains: one fixed formula unit in a pure substance versus variable proportions of two formula units in a mixture.

item.title: Determining the NaCl Contamination in a KCl Sample
item.stimulus:
A student is given a white solid labeled as pure potassium chloride, KCl. The student suspects that the solid is contaminated with sodium chloride, NaCl. An elemental analysis of a sample of the solid gives the results below. Assume that chlorine is present only as chloride in KCl and NaCl.

Quantity | Value
Mass of solid sample | 1.500 g
Mass of chlorine in sample | 0.7500 g

Molar masses (g/mol): Na 22.99; K 39.10; Cl 35.45; NaCl 58.44; KCl 74.55
item.model_answer:
(a) Mass percent Cl = (35.45 g/mol ÷ 74.55 g/mol) × 100 = 47.55%.

(b) The claim is supported. Measured mass percent Cl = (0.7500 g ÷ 1.500 g) × 100 = 50.00%. A pure substance contains only one type of formula unit, so its composition by mass is fixed; pure KCl must be 47.55% Cl. Because the sample is 50.00% Cl, it cannot be pure KCl and must be a mixture containing a substance with a higher chlorine fraction, such as NaCl.

(c) Let x = mass of NaCl. Then mass of KCl = 1.500 − x.
x(35.45/58.44) + (1.500 − x)(35.45/74.55) = 0.7500
0.60661x + 0.71328 − 0.47552x = 0.7500
0.13109x = 0.03672
x = 0.2801 g NaCl (and 1.220 g KCl).

(d) In both compounds each formula unit contains one Cl⁻ ion paired with one metal ion. A Na⁺ ion (about 22.99 amu) has much less mass than a K⁺ ion (about 39.10 amu), so a NaCl formula unit has a smaller total mass while containing the same chloride mass. Chlorine therefore makes up a larger fraction of the mass in NaCl (60.66%) than in KCl (47.55%).
item.verification_python:
Na=22.99;K=39.10;Cl=35.45
NaCl=58.44;KCl=74.55
assert abs(Na+Cl-NaCl)<0.01 and abs(K+Cl-KCl)<0.01
pK=Cl/KCl*100
assert abs(pK-47.55)<0.005
pNa=Cl/NaCl*100
assert abs(pNa-60.66)<0.005
meas=0.7500/1.500*100
assert abs(meas-50.00)<1e-9
assert meas>pK
a=Cl/NaCl;b=Cl/KCl
assert abs(a-0.60661)<1e-5 and abs(b-0.47552)<1e-5
assert abs(1.5*b-0.71328)<1e-5
assert abs((a-b)-0.13109)<1e-5
x=(0.7500-1.500*b)/(a-b)
assert abs(x-0.2801)<0.00005
assert abs((1.500-x)-1.220)<0.0005
assert abs((0.7500-1.5*b)-0.03672)<1e-5
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Elemental Analysis of a KCl Sample Contaminated with NaCl
item.stimulus:
A chemist receives a bottle labeled potassium chloride, KCl. She suspects the solid has been contaminated with sodium chloride, NaCl. She assumes the solid contains only KCl and NaCl. She dissolves a sample of the solid in water and precipitates all of the chloride. She uses the precipitate to find the mass of chlorine in the sample. Her results are shown below.

Quantity | Value
Mass of solid sample | 2.000 g
Mass of chlorine in sample | 0.9904 g

Molar masses (g/mol): K = 39.10, Na = 22.99, Cl = 35.45
item.model_answer:
(a) Molar mass of KCl = 39.10 + 35.45 = 74.55 g/mol. Mass percent Cl = (35.45 / 74.55) × 100 = 47.55%.

(b) Mass percent Cl in the sample = (0.9904 g / 2.000 g) × 100 = 49.52%. Every formula unit of KCl has one K and one Cl, so pure KCl always has the same composition, 47.55% Cl. The sample is 49.52% Cl, which is different. Therefore the sample is not pure KCl; it is a mixture.

(c) Let x = mass of NaCl, so the mass of KCl is (2.000 − x) g. The mass fraction of Cl in NaCl is 35.45/58.44 = 0.6066, and in KCl it is 0.4755.
0.6066x + 0.4755(2.000 − x) = 0.9904
0.1311x = 0.9904 − 0.9510 = 0.0394
x = 0.300 g NaCl
Mass percent NaCl = (0.300 g / 2.000 g) × 100 = 15.0%.

(d) SiO2 particles contain no chlorine atoms. Mixing them into KCl would add mass without adding any Cl, so the mass percent of Cl would be lower than 47.55%. The measured value is higher, 49.52%. Each NaCl formula unit also contains one Cl atom, but it pairs Cl with an Na atom (22.99 amu), which is lighter than a K atom (39.10 amu). As a result, NaCl is 60.66% Cl. Replacing some KCl formula units with NaCl formula units increases the number of Cl atoms per gram of sample. This raises the % Cl above 47.55%, which is consistent with the data.
item.verification_python:
K=39.10; Na=22.99; Cl=35.45
mKCl=K+Cl; mNaCl=Na+Cl
assert abs(mKCl-74.55)<1e-9
assert abs(mNaCl-58.44)<1e-9
fK=Cl/mKCl; fN=Cl/mNaCl
assert abs(fK*100-47.55)<0.01
assert abs(fN*100-60.66)<0.01
sample=2.000; mCl=0.9904
pct=mCl/sample*100
assert abs(pct-49.52)<0.001
assert pct>fK*100
x=(mCl-sample*fK)/(fN-fK)
assert abs(x-0.300)<0.001
assert abs(round(x,4)-0.3003)<1e-9
pctN=x/sample*100
assert abs(pctN-15.0)<0.05
assert abs(fN-0.6066)<0.0001 and abs(fK-0.4755)<0.0001
assert abs(2.000*0.4755-0.9510)<1e-9
assert abs(0.6066-0.4755-0.1311)<1e-9
assert abs(0.9904-0.9510-0.0394)<1e-9
assert abs(0.0394/0.1311-0.300)<0.001
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

Concludes that mixing in NaCl raises the % Cl above 47.55%, matching the measured 49.52%.
criteria.fix: Reason per formula unit: compare the Cl atom's mass to the total mass of each kind of particle, and predict which direction each impurity shifts % Cl.

item.title: Purity of a Limestone Sample from Its Calcium Content
item.stimulus:
A geologist analyzes a 2.000 g sample of powdered limestone. The sample is a mixture of only calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, and silicon dioxide, SiO₂. Silicon dioxide contains no calcium. Elemental analysis shows that the sample contains 0.7208 g of calcium. Use the molar masses below.

Substance | Molar mass (g/mol)
Ca | 40.08
CaCO₃ | 100.09
SiO₂ | 60.09

Answer the following.

parts.prompt: Calculate the percent by mass of calcium in pure CaCO₃.

criteria.text: Calculates 40.04% calcium by mass in pure CaCO₃.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the molar mass of Ca by the molar mass of CaCO₃ (40.08 ÷ 100.09) and reports 40.04%.
criteria.fix: For a pure compound, divide the mass of the element in one mole by the compound's molar mass, then multiply by 100.

parts.prompt: Explain how the elemental analysis data show that the limestone sample is not pure CaCO₃.

criteria.text: Shows that the sample's calcium content (36.04% Ca, or 0.7208 g Ca in 2.000 g) is less than that of pure CaCO₃ (40.04% Ca, or 0.8009 g Ca in 2.000 g), so the sample cannot be pure CaCO₃.
criteria.evidence: Response compares a calcium composition value obtained from the data with the corresponding value for pure CaCO₃, notes that they differ, and concludes that the sample contains another substance.
criteria.fix: Calculate the measured percent of the element and compare it with the fixed percent in the pure compound; a mismatch means a mixture.

parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of CaCO₃ in the 2.000 g sample.

criteria.text: Calculates 1.800 g of CaCO₃ in the sample.
criteria.evidence: Response attributes all of the calcium to CaCO₃ (for example 0.7208 g Ca ÷ 40.08 g/mol × 100.09 g/mol, or 0.7208 g ÷ 0.4004) and reports 1.800 g.
criteria.fix: All the calcium is in CaCO₃, so convert the calcium mass to moles of Ca, equal to moles of CaCO₃, then to grams.

parts.prompt: Calculate the ratio of the number of calcium atoms to the number of silicon atoms in the sample.

criteria.text: Calculates a Ca : Si atom ratio of 5.40 : 1.
criteria.evidence: Response finds the mass of SiO₂ (2.000 g − 1.800 g = 0.200 g), converts calcium and SiO₂ to amounts (0.01798 mol Ca and 3.33 × 10⁻³ mol Si), and reports 5.40 Ca atoms per Si atom, or a ratio consistent with the student's earlier answers.
criteria.fix: Find the other component's mass by subtraction, convert each element to moles, then divide, because mole ratios equal atom ratios.

item.model_answer:
(a) Percent Ca in CaCO₃ = (40.08 g/mol ÷ 100.09 g/mol) × 100% = 40.04%.

(b) Percent Ca in the sample = (0.7208 g ÷ 2.000 g) × 100% = 36.04%. Pure CaCO₃ always contains 40.04% Ca by mass, so 2.000 g of pure CaCO₃ would contain 0.8009 g of Ca. The measured value, 36.04%, is lower, so the sample cannot be pure CaCO₃; it must contain another substance (here SiO₂) mixed with the CaCO₃.

(c) Moles of Ca = 0.7208 g ÷ 40.08 g/mol = 0.01798 mol. Each formula unit of CaCO₃ contains one Ca atom, so there are 0.01798 mol of CaCO₃. Mass of CaCO₃ = 0.01798 mol × 100.09 g/mol = 1.800 g.

(d) Mass of SiO₂ = 2.000 g − 1.800 g = 0.200 g. Moles of SiO₂ = 0.200 g ÷ 60.09 g/mol = 3.33 × 10⁻³ mol, so there are 3.33 × 10⁻³ mol of Si atoms. Ratio Ca : Si = 0.01798 mol ÷ 3.33 × 10⁻³ mol = 5.40, so there are 5.40 calcium atoms for every silicon atom.
item.verification_python:
Ca,CaCO3,SiO2=40.08,100.09,60.09
assert abs(40.08+12.01+3*16.00-CaCO3)<1e-9
assert abs(28.09+2*16.00-SiO2)<1e-9
pct=Ca/CaCO3*100
assert abs(pct-40.04)<0.005
mCa,ms=0.7208,2.000
assert abs(mCa/ms*100-36.04)<0.005
assert abs(ms*Ca/CaCO3-0.8009)<0.00005
nCa=mCa/Ca
assert abs(nCa-0.01798)<0.000005
mCaCO3=nCa*CaCO3
assert abs(mCaCO3-1.800)<0.0005
assert abs(mCa/0.4004-1.800)<0.0005
mSiO2=ms-1.800
assert abs(mSiO2-0.200)<1e-9
nSi=mSiO2/SiO2
assert abs(nSi-3.33e-3)<0.005e-3
r=nCa/nSi
assert abs(r-5.40)<0.005
assert abs(0.01798/3.33e-3-5.40)<0.005
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')
